toc.title: Let it unite and ground us
Do some work, and give yourself rest

blocks.p: This day is going to end. I want to talk about that with you, and gently nudge you to take a concrete step forward in your self-improvement or trauma recovery goals now. I don't want you to end this day with regret about not doing anything differently. I want you to feel proud of yourself for doing something different, and I want to help you increase your motivation for making change in your life, no matter what that is.

This is a heavy topic, but a very important one, and in all honesty it connects to other important and potentially triggering topics. Time might actually be the most important topic I, or we, could ever address. Yet it's really not discussed, probably because it's difficult, and it can add pressure and stress.

So I'm going to give you an exit right now. If you don't want to think about time, life, and death, stop reading here and do whatever else you would typically do. If you choose to continue, expect that I'm going to discuss some heavy topics relating to time, life, death, and choices.

I'm also going to give you a suggestion, if you need it. It might be a good idea to do something right now that helps you feel calm and grounded in the present moment before we continue. Maybe something that uses your senses, something that connects you to your external environment. Once you have some, or enough, self-compassion, calm, and curiosity, then I'd recommend you continue, as long as you're still interested and curious.
This day is going to end, and you won't be able to get it back. The time you have left in it is finite, and 24 hours of your life will have gone by again.

Of course, the finiteness of time isn't related only to this day, but to life as well, the broader life. To put it bluntly, everything that is alive will die. That includes me, and yes, that includes you.

So what does this have to do with your self-improvement, and maybe even your trauma recovery? I'm going to guess that there's something you want to change in your life. Something you're probably frustrated with. Something you judge yourself for doing, potentially day after day.

Let's call this something your behavioral adaptation. Through the lens of the Polyvagal Theory, a behavioral adaptation is something you do to make yourself feel something different. Something you do to reduce whatever pain you have, probably.
It could be something personal:

ul: You don't want to feel depressed, so you use a drug.
Your chronic anxiety leads you to pick or pull at something to calm down, or pseudo calm down.
You temporarily resolve your shame through self-harm.
You binge eat instead of feeling alone.

blocks.p: A behavioral adaptation could also be something interpersonal:

ul: You can't live with your rage, so you take it out on loved ones.
Your intense inner anxiety is too much, so you obsessively focus on your kids.
You can't tolerate the depths of sorrow you feel as you watch your adult children waste their lives and accomplish nothing, so you try to appease them and pray something changes.

blocks.p: I share these examples because they're very real. There's a strong likelihood you can relate to one or more of them. On my end, there's no judgment in these examples, though I know, and I think you know, that you do judge yourself for whatever your behavioral adaptation is.

Let's get back to time, and to possibly changing these behavioral adaptations. If you'll allow me to be blunt again: the amount of time you have left to change that behavioral adaptation is lower now than when I began this sentence, and less than it was a minute ago. The number of days you have left to change that something is less now than yesterday. Time has gone by that you will never, ever get back.
Therefore, the urgency to make a change has increased. Less time, more urgency.

And on top of this, to make things even more urgent, you don't know how much time you have left. I personally tend to assume I'm going to live until I'm about 90, but in reality, I have no idea if that's going to happen. There's no guarantee on how much time I have left, or how much time you have left. That means whatever you want to change in life, such as your behavioral adaptation, has some date at which it will no longer be possible to change it. And we don't know what that date is.

So yes, there's a lot of urgency when it comes to these behavioral adaptations. This probably makes you uncomfortable, and it should. There is literally an endpoint to the time that you have left. You might believe in an afterlife, so I'll word it this way: there is an endpoint to the time you have left in this life. For my fellow non-believers, this is it. There's no comfort in an afterlife for us.

blocks.h: Let it unite and ground us

blocks.p: For all of us, the discomfort of death is heavy. It feels like anxiety. It feels like pressure, as it should. It's a very uncomfortable, very heavy topic, and I honestly don't know if there's a topic more important than our mortality.

In my opinion, this should mobilize us to take action and make change now. We should connect with one another in acknowledgment that we all have things to work on and a limited amount of time. Death and time should be things that unite us and keep us grounded in the present moment.

I tend to find the thought of death anxiety-producing at first, almost paralyzing, but only for a brief moment. Then my system self-regulates back into its safety state, and thoughts of appreciation come to mind. Appreciation for the people in my life, and for the opportunity to impact the world in a positive way, like through the podcast, even when dealing with a heavy topic like death and time. And also an appreciation for simply being alive.

However, you could totally ignore this uncomfortable truth and go watch bullshit on TikTok. Your anxious mind will be successfully distracted, your emotions will numb, and that'll be that. You'll have lost more time, yes, but you'll have spared yourself some discomfort.

You could make the choice to do nothing different in your life. You could choose to ignore this uncomfortable truth. You could totally do that, and honestly, I would not judge you whatsoever. I don't think you should judge yourself either. I would encourage you to take complete ownership of the way you choose to spend your time, right now and in the months ahead.

Two months from now, hopefully you're working on it, and things are getting better. Hopefully the adaptation is less intense and happening less often, and the emotions driving it are less intense as well. If that's the case, you'll have a lot to be proud of. Even if you're not perfectly satisfied with who you are and the choices you make, you'll have made progress, and you'll feel good about that.

blocks.h: Do some work, and give yourself rest

blocks.p: I don't think you need to constantly work on getting unstuck. But I do believe in two key things:

ol: Do some work on getting unstuck. I think it's worth it. The experience of relief, the reconnection with yourself, with your present moment, and maybe even with the people in your life, is worth it. Even a little bit of unstucking makes a big difference.

Give yourself rest from getting unstuck. You don't need to do the unstucking work constantly. Deliberately put in a little work each day, and then, yes, give yourself some time on TikTok if you like, or whatever your social media vice is. Or actual rest. Maybe you do need actual rest, like being mindfully still in silence, or granting yourself a moment of safety and connection by doing something you enjoy.

blocks.p: My goal here is not to scare you. My goal is to help you put things into perspective. Honestly, a very sobering one, and I encourage you to take action on it now.

Put something into practice that you've been learning and maybe never tried out. Now might be the time to hire a therapist or work with a coach, if you can, or even sign up for that course you've been eyeballing. I almost don't care what you do to make change in your life, as long as you're not harming yourself or somebody else.
Maybe the first step you take now is to follow those little safety impulses you have within you:

ul: If they're guiding you toward joining a flag football league, great.
If they're pulling you toward therapy, lovely.
If they're pulling you toward online courses, wonderful.
If the right step is joining a bicycling club, maybe now's the time to take a step forward.
If the next step is to plant little yellow flowers in front of your house, so you have something pleasant to look at when you come home from a miserable day of work, go have at it.
Maybe the next step is to reconnect with your family, or apologize for something.

blocks.p: Honestly, I don't care what it is. I just want to gently nudge you in the right direction, and only you'll know what that is.

I recorded this for the 200th episode of Stuck Not Broken, a big milestone. This is heavy stuff, and I'm glad you made it through and that you're here with me at the end of it. There's tons of hope, and I know you can take the step you need, starting now.
